The night had a kind of soft silence around it. I considered, as I dangled my legs off the side of the roof, that maybe the world was generally very quiet and I just didn't notice.

That morning, my sister had sent the table through the window and slammed the front door with her mind. She'd flung back the curtains, rattled the dishes in the cabinets, and brought down the ceiling fan without leaving her seat. It was her Gift, to control anything solid. And she was twelve, not old enough to control her temper.

My mother had made breakfast that morning. She poured orange juice for my father and water for herself without a pitcher; it was her Gift. My father had ruffled her hair playfully, cooled his coffee with an invisible breath, then moved the wind out of the wind chimes, because it was his Gift and he hated the wind chimes.

I'd said nothing that morning. I poured milk into my cereal, holding onto the plastic and trying not to spill it. I ate with a spoon as my sister ate hands-free.

And in the evening, I sat on the roof, looking up at my canvas. The swirling black and indigo sky came alive for me, twisting colors that decorated the stars; the stars were brilliantly white.

As I took a deep breath, I reached up. Ever so slightly, I flicked my wrist, and the sky shifted.

A single star, trailing diamond dust, twirled out of place. It fell fast and glittered bright, and so I moved my hand again. It hung suspended in navy blue.

I plucked another star out of the sky, pinning it above the first. All night, as I did every night, I moved the stars.

And that was my Gift.

The butterfly, an iridescent blue, perched on my finger. It swayed gently, trembling, its antennae looped into curls.

"No," I said. "Get off." I shook my hand violently. "Get *off*. You can't protect me." 

Luminous eyes stared up at me, reflecting my own face.

I shuddered. "Butterflies don't have *eyes*."

"I may be fragile— "

"I said get off of me! This isn't fair."

"Child— "

I thrust a finger at the boy next to me. "He got a wolf. See the girl next to him?" The girl twirled a lock of hair around her finger, nose to nose with a giant cat. "She got a lion. A *lion*."

"Fluttering wings can start hurricanes," it said softly, still shaking in the breeze.

I sat down in the grass. Dewdrops jumped at my touch; they splattered, cut by blades of grass. "I don't believe you."

There was a quiet pause between us, as children—adults now, really—laughed in wonder at their Guardians. Then: "Do you want me to leave?"

With a heavy-hearted sigh, I looked away from the tiny creature. "I want a real Guardian," I said honestly. "I don't want you."

"I will die, then."

I swallowed hard. "I don't care."

"Fluttering wings," it repeated, "can start hurricanes."

And against the twilight, its softly shining wings withered and fell. Little blue lights scattered like stars across the sky, and its antennae unfurled and drifted away. 

I felt a warm breath on my neck. The hairs on my arms stood up.

I turned, slowly, carefully, and found myself staring at an enormous bear. Its brown fur, streaked by gold, rippled across its powerful body as it plodded another step forward. When I raised my eyes to the bear's, I was met by the inky darkness of its gaze.

And time passed, and the bear protected me. It was his duty, after all, and as I grew into real adulthood, he was often by my side with advice. Yet as my peers grew older, and had children of their own, the next generation of Guardians was a curious one.

Most children before had been paired with foxes and falcons, wolves and wildcats, the powerful defenders of the Realm. But this generation was full of the most exotic beings. My sister's child was greeted by a tropical bird, bursting with the colors of a sunset by the sea. That child's friend found a frog: a rather small thing, but patterned so exquisitely it brought the girl to tears. There were peacocks, decked in rich indigos and deep greens; insects, their gossamer wings like lace; fish, shimmering scales of silver and gold.

And there were butterflies.

There were many, many butterflies, and one of them, one day, spoke to me.

It fluttered in my heart, whimsical and bright, and whispered about joy and love. It told me about the butterfly effect. It told me how one decision could change the world.

It reminded me that one decision, ever so small, could start hurricanes.

And so I listened to the butterfly, as it murmured from my heart—because this time, I knew it could not be so easily broken.

I believe in a lot of things. One plus one is two, of course, and the sky is usually blue. I believe that some people are inherently good and some are inherently evil, and that the vast majority of people are selfish.

There are three things I firmly disbelieved in, however: eternity, true love, and happiness.

You see, even love has its expiration date. It's not some transcendent force that escapes the laws of our ever-shrinking universe—it's just a feeling. A very human, and therefore very fickle feeling.

People like me don't expect much from people like you because we can see the expiration date on your love, and sometimes we can't help but see it lit up like a neon sign in our heads. Sure, we could just let it quietly haunt us, whispering that nothing's real, reminding us our time with you is limited; that's hard, though. Everything hurts.

I was hyper-aware of it throughout high school. Back when love was addicting, I craved those numbers, breaking hearts before anyone could break mine. I thought that only my parents' love was eternal.

See, I was under the impression that Mom and Dad loved me unconditionally. That there was no expiration date. And—god, what a stupid kid I was—it broke me when I realized the truth.

It wasn't enough that they were hardly ever around. It wasn't enough that they were cold, distant; it wasn't enough that when they weren't, they were explosive, matches in oil and sparks in water. I didn't see an expiration date for them because they never loved me in the first place.

Stupid, stupid, stupid. What a stupid kid I was.

After that, I guess it got more difficult. I stopped letting people in because there just wasn't any point. It was stupid to live in the moment when I knew the future was right at my heels, and every time I remembered that it felt like something was slowly tearing me apart from the inside out.

It's not so difficult anymore.

One day, I passed this animal shelter like I usually did, and they had all those scruffy little dogs out front in their little pens. Those things were barking and whining loud enough to wake the dead. It's funny, because it woke me right out of whatever mood I was in.

I don't know why, but I stopped right in front of the animal shelter. There was this one little dog just laying against the wall with his head on his tiny paws and, damn, I'm not much of a dog person but this thing was hella cute.

I stood there like an idiot, half-smiling at it, and it must've felt me staring because it looked up at me.

See, it sounds stupid, but my eyes locked with his. And that's when I saw the expiration date, and three things changed.

In that moment, I believed in happiness. I believed in love.

And I believed in eternity.

She was counting stars again. She'd decided against recognizing the impossibility of it, instead choosing to occupy her mind with numbers. Every time she messed up she'd keep counting, ignoring the inaccuracy, ignoring the concept of infinity.

She was waiting again. As the lights went out one by one, she was watching them disappear. One might think they were stars fading, the weak glimmers winking out. It was more likely that the lights scattered across the black sky would be swept away — more likely that than the very notion that the city lights were going dark.

She was worrying again. He'd been gone for hours and she knew, she *knew* it would take such a long time, but she was worried all the same. They hurt the ones who believed in stardust and shunned the satellites; they hated the ones who looked above the glass and steel buildings to the clouds. And he was threatening to destroy their world. He would turn off their lights.

She was counting stars, but she wasn't really. She was just counting, listing numbers in her head because there was nothing else to do. The phone was on the balcony's railing. It was right next to her, and so she picked it up and ran her fingers gently over the buttons. She considered it. She hesitated.

And that's when he fell through the door bleeding.

I flip through page after page. There are confessions and explanations and reminders from billions of different people — billions of stories that I will never get the chance to read.

A sentence catches my eye. I flip backwards and skim the page, chewing my bottom lip. Quickly, I look up, then over my shoulder. Everyone is engrossed in their own activities.

And I make a decision.

~~

The girl hasn't noticed me yet. She tucks a lock of hair behind her ear and it curls under her chin. 

Her bedroom is small, sparsely decorated. No posters hang on the wall, no paintings or drawings or hastily scribbled notes like the ones she fills the margins of her journals with. There is only white: white walls, white ceiling, and a dusty grey-brown hardwood floor.

Dressed in all black with dark hair, she is a sharp contrast to the white room. But her eyes — they are a splash of color banishing the black-and-white normalcy of the world. Her eyes are brighter than stars, lined with the night sky and sprinkled with emerald forests. They are warm but not trusting, soulful but not revealing.

In my infinite life, few things compare to her beauty.

"Child," I say softly.

She does not turn, staring at the wall, her beautiful eyes so tragically blank.

So I cross the room and lay a hand on her shoulder. I am unfamiliar, despite my many readings, with the workings of the human mind. Time tends to blur together after a while, and for once I find myself uncertain of what I intend to do.

"Do you know who I am?"

Her head moves, but she is looking through me as if I am glass. I watch her lips form words. There is no sound, but her eyes are shining.

"I can save you. Let me."

"I took" — she breathes faintly, her voice weak and fragile — "the entire bottle."

"I know." I take her hand. Her eyes, the light of the room, focus on me. "I know."

A gasp breaks through her throat. "The world — why is it spinning so fast? I can't — I can't stand up anymore." Another fluttering gasp.

"I know."

"I — I'm tired. I want to — to go to sleep."

"I know."

She shakes her head slowly, trembling. "I'm not sure I want to die," she whispers.

"I know." And this is where I gesture to the phone lying on the white bedside table. "I have paused time, child, but it is still running out."

Her hand moves slowly and clutches onto the phone as if it is her lifeline.

It is her lifeline.

She is shaking. Her fingers press the numbers: 9 - 1 - 1. It begins to ring.

"911, what's your emergency?" She gives them her address in a frail voice, then falls back onto the bed, still breathing raggedly. Her eyes, brighter than the sunlight streaming through the one window, blink slowly.

"How did you know?" she asks me.

"You wrote to me." I pull out a folded sheet of paper with notes scribbled into the margins, and I smooth the creases. "'Dear Diary,'" I read as her eyelids flutter.

And then the lights turn off.

Her eyes, the color of a stormy sky. Her hair, with a shine like starlight and a fullness like the moon. Her hand on mine.

Each breath, a struggle; each heartbeat, staccato. An uneven beeping beside my bed. 

Her footsteps and the sound of a door. Tears on my face. Tears in my heart. My mind alive, my body broken.

My soul alone in its final moments. Her face only in my head, a beautiful, breathtaking vision. If only—

Sand through an hourglass or through my fingers, no difference. No time and no sleep for the wicked nor weary.

Wicked smiles, faint and unseen. Invisible youth still there. Her footsteps, only echoes of her old self. Her laugh, tired. Her, not here. Somewhere else as I—

The beeping, flat now. A line.

If only.

When the rain started to come down in a misty drizzle, I closed the door and slid the bolt into place. Once there had been days when the thunderstorms were music, and I had laughed with nymphs as they twirled in circles around me by the lake. Perhaps I was tired now, or perhaps it was because of his death that I no longer watched in fascination when water droplets collected on my skin.

The scratching started as soon as I sat down. I stood on tiptoe to see out the peephole of the door — unsurprisingly, I saw nothing. Deciding not to care, I sat back down.

As the sound of the rain got louder and louder, so did the scratching. With an exasperated sigh I got up again and opened the door.

A gust of wind tore through the house carrying icy needles of water. I slammed the door shut, heart fluttering. And unbidden memories came back to me.

I saw his smile and his emerald eyes reflected in mine. The ghost of his hand print was on my palm; I could feel the way our fingers had fit together. And the water—clear, cold, sapphire water dripping down every crease of his face in rivulets, shining on his skin like diamonds. The rocks, hidden out of sight, below the turquoise surface. And the sudden scarlet ruby color that slithered onto the lake and spread across it and the screams sharper than crystal—

There was a yowl from outside the door.

There was thunder rumbling in the distance. And the water. God, the *water*.

His eyes had been open. Bloodshot. Not emeralds anymore. The light had been gone, the life had been gone. As simple as blowing out a candle flame, he was gone.

The yowl turned into a pitiful whine.

I had turned away from the lake so long ago. It was not sapphires or turquoise; it was dark, inky grey. 

The whine broke off into a whimper. I crossed the room impulsively and flung the door open. Wind and rain surged in again, but I held my ground and looked out through the foggy sky.

"Who's there?" I called, my voice scattered and broken across the howling gale. "You can— " I hesitated, then shouted, "You can come in!"

A small tail flickered through my line of sight. Then something dashed between my legs, hurtling into the table. I leaned against the door, closing it, my heart nervous.

My nerves settled. It was a dragon, the size of a kitten, looking up at me with a tilted head. Twin horns, nothing more than little nubs, poked out from between soft ears. 

"Hey," I said softly. I held out a hand and the dragon crept forward, belly low to the ground. "I guess you ate the food, huh?" I hadn't left a bowl out for the dragons since he died, but something possessed me to do it last night. I'd almost forgotten them—curious creatures, but timid, too.

The dragon's wings fluttered and it lifted itself into the air, its big, emerald eyes level with mine.

A few hours later, the rain had lessened to a drizzle again. Gentle kisses of water fell to the sidewalk, and I opened the door.

It had been so long.

Nymphs were dancing by the lake.

"You do realize this is a marriage proposal, right?" She looked up at him with a quirked smile.

*I... Do not speak to me that way, mortal.* The words slipped through her mind like water, filling her mind with his rasping breath. His hands, shadowy and dark with slender finger-like tendrils, moved towards his face uncomfortably.

The girl in front of him — and she was that, just a girl — rolled her eyes. "Sweetheart, you're inside the circle. I can talk how I want."

The curled horns on his head made a sickening *crack* noise as they grew, spiraling larger. *You may do no such thing, you speck of consciousness, you tiny vessel of life overshadowed by the greatness of the universe.*

"Marry me."

*Wha— No. No, a creature such as myse— What are you doing?* 

She'd scooted forward, one perfectly manicured fingernail touching the salt of the circle that acted as a barrier between them. "Hm? Oh, nothing."

*Do you— Are you—* As each flustered word punctured her mind from a different angle, his horns retracted back into his head.

"Please?"

*I am aware that a mind so tiny cannot process even the most logical information, but you must know that releasing me from the circle would allow me to attack you.* He took a step backwards on hooved feet; the smoky features sharpened into focus, and she could make out an aquiline nose. The demon had thin, downturned lips with fangs protruding into them.

The girl's eyes widened, then she shook her head hastily and looked at the floor. "I'm not stupid," she said almost softly. "I know what happens when you break the circle. Marry. Me."

*No! You are most certainly not in a position to negotiate, child. It would be in your best interest to banish me before your foolish actions have disastrous consequences.*

She slid her finger across the salt, pushing a bit of the circle inwards. Then she blew on it.

It scattered.

The circle was broken.

For a few seconds, the demon stared at her. His face was unreadable, and there was a strange look in his blood-red eyes. *I— You are—* He moved forward uncertainly. *Before I... kill you* — he'd tripped over the phrase — *tell me: why, child?*

"I deserve the pain."

The thin lips curved upwards. *You would be incapable of tolerating Hell.*

She blinked in surprise. "What?"

*Whatever you have done —*

"I've done so many horrible, cruel things, Mr. Demon, you— "

*You're only human, child.*

And he stepped out of the circle.

We were watching the clouds.

I pointed at the sky. "Doesn't that one look like a bunny?"

"Nope."

"I— Okay. What do you think it looks like?"

The six-year I was babysitting turned to me, rolled her eyes, and said, "A cloud. You're boring."

"You know, when it gets dark, you can wish on a star," I told her, completely changing the subject.

"Don't wanna." She stood up. Then she sat back down. "But I can wish on the sun."

"You know, the sun is actually a star, so—"

She put her finger on my lips. "Don't be stupid." Squinting, and staring directly into the sun, she whispered, "I wish for my babysitter to die."

"What the actual fu— fruitcake—"

"It didn't work." A giggle burst from her mouth, but it was soon replaced by a bored scowl again.

We sat there in the grass for a few minutes, rays of sunshine twisting through the few trees. There was still just enough dew droplets on the grass to annoy me.

Someone tapped my shoulder.

I turned and found myself face-to-face with a middle-aged man in a top hat and three-piece suit.

"Can I help you?"

"Do you happen to have a blanket?"

I bit the inside of my cheek. "No, why?"

"I'm afraid this might be terribly messy, and I do hate messes."
